GO TO SITE MSF Access CRASH Based in Paris, CRASH conducts and directs studies and analysis of MSF actions. They participate in internal training sessions and assessment missions in the field. GO TO SITE CRASH UREPH Based in Geneva, UREPH (or Research Unit) aims to improve the way MSF projects are implemented in the field and to participate in critical thinking on humanitarian and medical action. GO TO SITE UREPH ARHP Based in Barcelona, ARHP documents and reflects on the operational challenges and dilemmas faced by the MSF field teams. GO TO SITE ARHP MSF Analysis Based in Brussels, MSF Analysis intends to stimulate reflection and debate on humanitarian topics organised around the themes of migration, refugees, aid access, health policy and the environment in which aid operates. GO TO SITE MSF Analysis MSF Supply This logistical and supply centre in Brussels provides storage of and delivers medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions. GO TO SITE MSF Supply MSF Logistique This supply and logistics centre in Bordeaux, France, provides warehousing and delivery of medical equipment, logistics and drugs for international purchases for MSF missions. GO TO SITE MSF Logistique Amsterdam Procurement Unit This logistical centre in Amsterdam purchases, tests, and stores equipment including vehicles, communications material, power supplies, water-processing facilities and nutritional supplements. GO TO SITE Amsterdam Procurement Unit Brazilian Medical Unit BRAMU specialises in neglected tropical diseases, such as dengue and Chagas, and other infectious diseases. This medical unit is based in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. GO TO SITE Brazilian Medical Unit MSF Medical Guidelines Our medical guidelines are based on scientific data collected from MSF’s experiences, the World Health Organization (WHO), other renowned international medical institutions, and medical and scientific journals. GO TO SITE MSF Medical Guidelines Epicentre Providing epidemiological expertise to underpin our operations, conducting research and training to support our goal of providing medical aid in areas where people are affected by conflict, epidemics, disasters, or excluded from health care. GO TO SITE Epicentre Evaluation Units Evaluation Units have been established in Vienna, Stockholm, and Paris, assessing the potential and limitations of medical humanitarian action, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of our medical humanitarian work. GO TO SITE Evaluation Units LGBTQI+ Inclusion in Health Settings MSF works with LGBTQI+ populations in many settings over the last 25-30 years. LGBTQI+ people face healthcare disparities with limited access to care and higher disease rates than the general population. GO TO SITE LGBTQI+ Inclusion in Health Settings LUXOR The Luxembourg Operational Research (LuxOR) unit coordinates field research projects and operational research training, and provides support for documentation activities and routine data collection. GO TO SITE LUXOR Intersectional Benchmarking Unit The Intersectional Benchmarking Unit collects and analyses data about local labour markets in all locations where MSF employs people. GO TO SITE Intersectional Benchmarking Unit MSF Academy for Healthcare To upskill and provide training to locally-hired MSF staff in several countries, MSF has created the MSF Academy for Healthcare. GO TO SITE MSF Academy for Healthcare Humanitarian Law This Guide explains the terms, concepts, and rules of humanitarian law in accessible and reader-friendly alphabetical entries. GO TO SITE Humanitarian Law MSF Paediatric Days The MSF Paediatric Days is an event for paediatric field staff, policy makers and academia to exchange ideas, align efforts, inspire and share frontline research to advance urgent paediatric issues of direct concern for the humanitarian field. GO TO SITE MSF Paediatric Days MSF Foundation The MSF Foundation aims to create a fertile arena for logistics and medical knowledge-sharing to meet the needs of MSF and the humanitarian sector as a whole. GO TO SITE MSF Foundation DNDi A collaborative, patients’ needs-driven, non-profit drug research and development organisation that is developing new treatments for neglected diseases, founded in 2003 by seven organisations from around the world. GO TO SITE DNDi MSF Science Portal Our digital portal dedicated to sharing the latest medical evidence from our humanitarian activities around the globe. GO TO SITE MSF Science Portal Noma Noma is a preventable and treatable neglected disease, but 90 per cent of people will die within the first two weeks of infection if they do not receive treatment. GO TO SITE Noma TIC The TIC is aiming to change how MSF works to better meet the evolving needs of our patients. GO TO SITE TIC Telemedicine MSF's telemedicine hub aims to overcome geographic barriers for equitable, accessible, and quality patient care. GO TO SITE Telemedicine Sweden Innovation Unit Launched in 2012, the MSF Sweden Innovation Unit deploys a human-centered approach for promoting a culture of innovation within MSF. GO TO SITE Sweden Innovation Unit Geo MSF The GeoMSF platform is a dynamic one-stop-shop website for all of MSF's GIS related services and products. Access maps and applications through the catalogue, request geographical support, or produce a map on GeoMSF. The ward has 50 chairs where cancer patients, regardless of the type of cancer, receive chemotherapy. By CONSTANT SAME BAGALWA - Associated Press 2 min read Health workers who are members of the safe and dignified burial team prepare to bury Abineno Justine, a 38 year old woman who died of the Ebola virus, in Bunia, Congo, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026. Dieudonne Dirole - AP Loading Audio Player By Instaread, Please Wait... http://www.bozemandailychronicle.com offers audio versions of articles using Instaread. Some words may be mispronounced. BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Congo on Saturday began vaccinating healthcare staff against Ebola in Bunia, the epicenter of the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history as they are “particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response,” the provincial governor said. Health workers and other front-line workers in the Ebola response are being prioritized to receive the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type of virus. Clinical trials are ongoing to find a licensed vaccine for the current outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no licensed vaccine or treatment. The rollout is targeting the Bunia and Mongbwalu zones in Ituri province, health authorities said Saturday. Both areas are among the hardest-hit by the virus. “Our collective duty is to protect life. Launching this vaccination drive for front-line staff in Ituri is not an arbitrary choice, as these workers are particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response,” the military governor of Ituri, Maj. Gen. Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, said Saturday. The campaign in Ituri and North Kivu is expected to cover 20,000 front-line workers over a period of six to nine months. As of Saturday, the country had recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, according to government figures, while 1,823 people have recovered. The outbreak is concentrated in Ituri province and is known to be the deadliest of all past 17 Ebola outbreaks in the country. The outbreak is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers’ strike and intense population movements. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Dr. Jeannot Elua, whom The Associated Press met at a health facility in Bunia, said the vaccine was “beneficial.” “We healthcare workers don’t really have a choice: we are going to receive it,” he said. “Some people here had already received the previous vaccine. I received it myself, because it was mandatory.” Another front-line health worker, Dr. Jean Paul Uzele, who was vaccinated with Ervebo during the 10th Ebola outbreak, said it was unclear to him whether he should get vaccinated again. “If it arrives, we will receive it too," he said. “But the question is whether we need to be vaccinated a second time." Last month, the Ervebo vaccine was rolled out in Kisangani in the Tshopo province. The campaign was expected to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces. The use of Ervebo is taking place in a specific scientific context. The vaccine is licensed for use against Ebola virus disease caused by the Zaire strain — a different, more common type of Ebola virus. The World Health Organization said last month that 70,000 doses of Ervebo were approved for use in Congo. About 50,000 doses are intended for front-line and health workers, while 20,000 doses will be used in a clinical trial to study whether the vaccine protects against Bundibugyo virus, which is causing the current outbreak and has no licensed vaccine or treatment. The vaccine is being used under a compassionate-use program, which allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use. Health authorities said Ervebo could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus because the two viruses are related. But whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. records.content_title: Congo faces unprecedented Ebola outbreak without approved vaccine protection
records.content: As the Ebola outbreak spreads unabated in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), vaccine developers are scrambling to develop and test a vaccine candidate that will target the species at its center. The outbreak, which has become the largest ever recorded in the country, is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus, for which there is no approved vaccine. On 30 July, the vaccine alliance CEPI announced it was providing funding of up to US$8.5 million for Hilleman Laboratories to advance the development of a Bundibugyo Ebola vaccine and produce doses for human testing. Hilleman Laboratories is a Singapore-based vaccine manufacturer established by US biopharmaceutical company MSD and the health-focused charitable foundation Wellcome. The vaccine candidate under development originated from the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative, IAVI and WHO scientists identified it in May as the most promising so far. The first doses are expected to be ready for clinical trials by the end of the year. Meanwhile, however, the outbreak is moving with “unprecedented speed”, according to WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. How bad is the outbreak? As of 7 September, WHO reported 6,757 confirmed cases and 3,267 deaths, giving the outbreak a case-fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. The outbreak has spread across six provinces. Ituri remains the main focus, while substantial transmission continues in North Kivu and Haut-Uélé. Cases have also been reported in South Kivu, Tshopo and Bas-Uélé. As well as being the largest Ebola outbreak of any species recorded in the DRC, it is the second-largest globally, after the 2014-16 West Africa epidemic, which killed more than 11,300 people. The current outbreak has grown unusually quickly. The WHO’s 14 August update said is was “expanding faster than any previous Ebola outbreak”. Tedros told an emergency committee on 18 August that the epidemic was “far from being under control”. Children make up roughly a quarter of cases but nearly a third of deaths, according to the UN children’s agency UNICEF. Meanwhile, 155 health workers have been infected, 45 of whom have died, according to the WHO. A WHO investigation suggests the outbreak began in mid-January, about four months before it was declared, after early cases were mistaken for malaria and typhoid. Why is there no approved vaccine yet? Every licensed Ebola vaccine, including MSD’s single-dose Ervebo, targets the Zaire species - not Bundibugyo, which was first identified during an outbreak in Uganda in 2007. records.content: The Ebola outbreak has frightened patients away from clinics in Ituri in the DRC, threatening the lives of people living with HIV and other conditions. As the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) confronts its 17th and fastest-growing Ebola outbreak, a troubling warning is emerging from community networks in Ituri province. These networks, which support people living with HIV, are reporting an unexpected number of deaths among people living with HIV. The Africa Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and UNAIDS are working with national authorities to verify these reports. But the message is already clear: while Ebola is claiming headlines, another health crisis could be unfolding in its shadow. This is a lesson Africa has learned before. Epidemics do not only kill through infection. They also kill when health systems become overwhelmed, clinics empty, medicine supplies are disrupted, and people are too frightened or unable to seek care. Falling clinic attendance For people living with HIV, continuity of treatment is not optional. Antiretroviral therapy must be taken consistently to keep people healthy and prevent drug resistance. When treatment is interrupted, health can deteriorate rapidly, leaving people vulnerable to opportunistic infections and more severe outcomes from other diseases. That is why the current Ebola outbreak demands a broader response than Ebola control alone. The warning signs are already visible in Ituri. Clinic attendance is falling. Laboratory and health system capacity is being redirected toward Ebola. Insecurity is limiting outreach efforts. At the same time, previous cuts to health, HIV and community programmes have reduced response capacity when it is needed most. This matters because HIV remains a significant public health issue in the province. According to the DRC’s latest Demographic and Health Survey, an estimated 1.9% of the population in Ituri is living with HIV, representing thousands of people who depend on uninterrupted access to treatment, care and support. HIV cannot be treated as a secondary concern during an Ebola emergency. For those affected, it is a matter of life and death. The good news is that solutions already exist. Community-led organizations Across Ituri, community-led organizations are helping to prevent a wider health crisis. Supported by repurposed funding from UNAIDS and working alongside local authorities, a national network of people living with HIV (UCOP+), and a national civil society consortium (ANORS) are tracing people who have stopped attending clinics, connecting them to care, and ensuring access to multi-month treatment supplies. In Bunia and other heavily affected health zones, they are also combating misinformation, reducing stigma and referring people with warning signs of Ebola to treatment centers for testing. These efforts demonstrate a key lesson from Africa’s public health experience: communities are not simply beneficiaries of health programmes. They are essential to the response. People living with HIV and their organizations have spent decades building trust, reaching vulnerable populations and supporting treatment adherence. During emergencies, that trust becomes a critical public health asset. Community networks can identify people who have dropped out of care, deliver accurate information, support referrals and help maintain essential services when health systems are under strain. Yet these networks remain underfunded, only reaching only a fraction of those who need them. The DRC government’s decision to provide free healthcare during the Ebola response was an important step. The challenge now is ensuring that this commitment translates into reliable access across affected communities. Free healthcare must include uninterrupted HIV prevention, treatment and care. Policies alone will not save lives if medicines do not reach patients and community responders lack the resources to do their work. A patient cured of Ebola virus disease gets certificates from a health worker at the Ebola Treatment Center at Bunia General Reference Hospital. The experience of Esther Nyamungu, a community worker in Bunia, illustrates what is possible. Living with HIV herself, she contracted Ebola and survived. She attributes her survival to seeking treatment early and remaining adherent to her HIV medication. Her story should not be the exception. It should be the norm. Too often, disease programmes are treated as separate silos. But patients do not experience health challenges one disease at a time. Someone with HIV who contracts Ebola requires integrated care. Clear nationally agreed clinical pathways, including early HIV assessment and testing during Ebola treatment, can help prevent avoidable deaths and improve outcomes for both conditions. The DRC’s shift toward a village-centred and community-led Ebola response offers a valuable opportunity. Existing networks of people living with HIV can strengthen disease surveillance, support treatment continuity and help deliver accurate information to communities. But if we expect them to play these roles, we must provide adequate training, protection, and financing. Maintaining essential health services The country’s revised multisectoral Ebola response plan provides a platform for action and a direct call for partner support. We know what works. Multi-month dispensing of HIV medicines, community-led service delivery and strong referral systems prove effective in maintaining care during crises. The real challenge is implementing these approaches at scale and funding them adequately. This is ultimately a question of priorities. Saving lives from Ebola and maintaining essential health services are not competing goals. They are part of the same mission. If we focus solely on Ebola, we risk losing lives to preventable interruptions in HIV treatment and other essential services. If we protect both, we can emerge from this crisis with stronger, more resilient health systems and healthier communities. The DRC has the expertise, the leadership and the community networks needed to achieve both objectives. What is required now is the political will and financial commitment to ensure that no one is left behind. When Ebola strikes, HIV care cannot stop. Lives depend on it. Dr Jean Kaseya is the Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Winnie Byanyima is the Executive Director of The Joint United Nations Programme on HIV and AIDS (UNAIDS). Dr Samuel Roger Kamba is the Minister of Public Health in the Democratic Republic of Congo. (Dieudonne Dirole / Associated Press) By Constant Same Bagalwa Sept. 19, 2026 7:10 PM PT 4 min Click here to listen to this article Share via Close extra sharing options Email Facebook X LinkedIn Threads Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link URL Copied! Print 0:00 0:00 1x This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here. Congo has begun vaccinating front-line healthcare workers in Bunia, the epicenter of the world’s fastest-growing Ebola outbreak. Health workers are receiving the Ervebo shot, a vaccine effective against a different Ebola strain than the Bundibugyo virus, which is driving this outbreak and has no licensed vaccine or treatment. The campaign aims to inoculate 20,000 front-line staff over nine months. BUNIA, Congo — Congo on Saturday began vaccinating healthcare workers against Ebola in Bunia, the epicenter of the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history, as they are “particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response,” the provincial governor said. Health workers and other front-line workers in the Ebola response are being prioritized to receive the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type of virus. Clinical trials are ongoing to find a licensed vaccine for the current outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no licensed vaccine or treatment. The rollout is targeting the Bunia and Mongbwalu zones in Ituri province, health authorities said Saturday. Both areas are among the hardest-hit by the virus. Advertisement “Our collective duty is to protect life. Launching this vaccination drive for front-line staff in Ituri is not an arbitrary choice, as these workers are particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response,” the military governor of Ituri, Maj. Gen. Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, said Saturday. The campaign in Ituri and North Kivu is expected to cover 20,000 front-line workers over six to nine months. As of Saturday, the country had recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, according to government figures, while 1,823 people have recovered. The outbreak is known to be the deadliest of all past 17 Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Advertisement The outbreak is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, including war, insecurity, displacement, a health workers’ strike and intense population movements. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-16 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Dr. Jeannot Elua, whom the Associated Press met at a health facility in Bunia, said the vaccine was “beneficial.” “We healthcare workers don’t really have a choice. We are going to receive it,” he said. “Some people here had already received the previous vaccine. I received it myself, because it was mandatory.” Another front-line health worker, Dr. Jean Paul Uzele, who was vaccinated with Ervebo during the 10th Ebola outbreak, said it was unclear to him whether he should get vaccinated again. “If it arrives, we will receive it too,” he said. “But the question is whether we need to be vaccinated a second time.” Last month, the Ervebo vaccine was rolled out in Kisangani, in Tshopo province. The campaign was expected to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces. Advertisement The use of Ervebo is taking place in a specific scientific context. The vaccine is licensed for use against Ebola virus disease caused by the Zaire strain. The WHO said last month that 70,000 doses of Ervebo were approved for use in Congo. About 50,000 doses are intended for front-line and health workers, while 20,000 doses will be used in a clinical trial to study whether the vaccine protects against Bundibugyo virus. The vaccine is being used under a compassionate-use program, which allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use. Health authorities said Ervebo could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus because the two viruses are related. But whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied. Bagalwa writes for the Associated Press. records.content: News World MSF launches Ebola vaccine study in DR Congo — Anadolu Agency UA.NEWS 19 September 2026 16:15 International humanitarian medical organization Doctors Without Borders (MSF) has launched a study in the Democratic Republic of Congo to assess whether the Ervebo vaccine can provide protection against the Bundibugyo virus. The program in Ituri and North Kivu provinces will involve 20,000 healthcare workers and frontline workers who face an increased risk of contact with the virus. As reported by Anadolu Agency , the study was launched at a World Health Organization training center for healthcare workers in Bunia, the administrative center of Ituri province. It will last from nine to 12 months: three months will be allocated to vaccination, while participants will be monitored for at least six months. Vaccine for the study Last month, DR Congo authorities began an Ebola vaccination campaign among healthcare workers and frontline workers. The country was allocated 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine from the global stockpile of vaccines against Ebola virus disease for a Phase 3 clinical trial. Currently, no vaccine or specific treatment against the Bundibugyo virus has been approved. Ervebo is licensed and recommended for use during outbreaks of disease caused by the Ebola virus, formerly known as Zaire ebolavirus. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . MSF epidemiologist and deputy director of operations Gaigai Manangama said that Ervebo was initially not developed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus, but preliminary data indicate that it may provide some level of protection. Scale of the outbreak According to the latest data from the DR Congo Ministry of Health, 7,541 infections have been confirmed in the current outbreak, of which 3,639 ended in death. The epidemic has affected 62 health zones in seven provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, and South Ubangi. MSF noted that despite a decrease in hospitalizations and a slowdown in virus transmission, cases are emerging and spreading in new, insufficiently prepared areas. The organization also reported that basic response measures have still not been introduced in the primary outbreak hotspots. Read us on Telegram and Sends Download our app

Send Close Zoonotic Diseases Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print SEPTEMBER 18, 2026 DRC Bundibugyo Ebola Cases Over 7k By Carlyn Annunziata and Meaghan Lee Callaghan The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is spreading at an unprecedented rate. Source: Adobe Stock. As of Sept. 12, 7,200 cases and 3,475 deaths have been confirmed in the DRC, along with one exported case in France. Related Content Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak Tops 1,100 Confirmed Cases The Ebola outbreak continues to grow at rates not previously seen in northeastern regions of the DRC and Uganda. Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak Could Be One of Largest on Record The ongoing Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the DRC and Uganda could become one of the largest Ebola disease ... Uptick of Yellow Fever Continues in 2026 Mounting cases of yellow fever in the Americas have continued, alongside sustained transmission activity reported ... Meanwhile, response efforts in neighboring Uganda have managed to prevent community transmission. Since July 28, 20 cases and two deaths have been confirmed in Uganda. This is the DRC’s 17th Ebola outbreak since the virus was first identified in 1976, which makes it the country’s largest recorded Ebola outbreak, exceeding the 3,323 confirmed cases reported from the previously largest outbreak between 2018 and 2020. According to CDC, this is the second largest outbreak recorded worldwide, and it is growing at an unprecedented rate. In an Sept. 10 Disease Outbreak News report, the WHO announced that total number of affected health zones is 61, across six out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, and Tshopo. The Ituri province remains the most impacted, accounting more than 5,400 cases, or about 75% of all cases. The WHO is reporting a crude case fatality ratio of 48.3%. However, at least 1,611 patients have recovered as of Sept. 7, including 1,590 in the DRC, 18 in Uganda, two in Germany (patients who had been transported there for treatment), and one in France. Response efforts are challenging due to limited access to healthcare and diagnostic and laboratory services, according to the WHO. Conflict in outbreak areas has led to increased access restrictions to supplies needed for infection prevention and control and contact tracing. Healthcare workers are at risk of becoming infected due to violence and shortages in personal protective equipment. The risk for cross-border transmission into Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and other neighboring regions is high due to increased population movement and travel. Misinformation and distrust in the government further complicates communication and reporting efforts. Symptoms and Complications Bundibugyo virus, a severe type of Ebola virus, is a zoonotic disease. Transmission occurs when humans come into close contact with the blood or secretions from infected bats or non-human primates (BMJ 2014;349:g7348). Human-to-human transmission occurs when individuals come into direct contact with blood, organs, secretions, and other fluids from infected individuals or surfaces and materials contaminated with Ebola. On average, early symptoms present between eight to 10 days but may develop between two and 21 days following exposure to the virus. These early symptoms, also known as dry symptoms, include fever, muscle and joint aches, severe headache, fatigue and weakness, sore throat, and loss of appetite. Dry symptoms may develop into more severe or wet symptoms as the disease progresses. Wet symptoms usually occur four to five days after the initial symptoms occur and include unexplained bleeding, nausea, pain in the abdomen, diarrhea, and vomiting. Other symptoms, such as chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, red eyes, skin rash, hiccups, and seizures may also occur. Mortality is associated with a high viral load and early development of symptoms. In general, death occurs between six to 16 days from the onset of symptoms and is the result of shock and failure of multiple organs. Survival and recovery are usually seen in patients who experience an isolated fever for several days. Patients who do recover begin to improve around six to 11 days after the onset of symptoms. Mortality rates are highest for children under 5 years of age and adults older than 40. Survivors of Ebola may experience long-term complications, which include fatigue, headaches, muscle and joint pain, eye and vision problems, weight gain, stomach pain or appetite loss, memory loss, neck swelling, dry mouth, tightness of the chest, hair loss, hearing problems, pain or tingling in the hands and feet, inflammation of the tissues around the heart, testicular inflammation, menstrual changes, impotence, little or no interest in sex, sleep disturbances, depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder. The Response WHO and DRC health authorities continue to work together to implement a six-month response plan known as the Continental Preparedness and Response Plan to support emergency coordination and disease surveillance measures, laboratory testing, infection prevention and control, clinical care, community engagement, research, provide logistics and support for essential healthcare services, and improve response operations in affected and high-risk areas. Efforts are underway to address critical gaps in funding by engaging donors and mobilizing resources. The second meeting of the WHO’s International Health Regulations Emergency Committee on the epidemic of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the DRC also released temporary recommendations on Aug. 24. The CDC has deployed around 500 employees for this outbreak, including 120 people on site in the affected countries. WHO has advised against travel to and trade with affected countries. CDC has stated that no cases have been reported in the United States and the likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States remains low. What You Should Do CDC encourages individuals to contact their healthcare provider or state health department as soon as possible if they are experiencing symptoms and believe they have come in contact with someone infected with the Ebola virus. records.content: You need to enable JavaScript to run this app. Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus German politicsAIRussia Latest audioLatest videos Live TV Advertisement HealthDemocratic Republic of Congo Ebola: DR Congo outbreak not slowing, MSF warns Mark Hallam with AFP 09/18/2026September 18, 2026 Doctors Without Borders has warned against premature optimism amid the DRC's largest-ever Ebola outbreak. "The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving," an MSF official said, entering new and more underprepared regions. https://p.dw.com/p/5MsK7 Copy link Medical workers have tried to promote dignified burials that nevertheless minimize post-mortem transmission Image: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said on Friday that "the race to contain the Ebola disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is far from over." MSF issued the comments after DRC's government and the World Health Organization (WHO) had both spoken of signs of slowing transmission in some places earlier this week, prompting some relatively upbeat headlines and coverage. The outbreak, which was first declared in mid-May but likely started spreading several months earlier, is the largest in DRC's national history and the fastest-spreading on record anywhere. Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 02:31 What did MSF say about the outbreak and its spread? MSF — which has around 1,700 staff in the DRC, most of them Congolese — warned that while the observed spread was slowing in the initial epicenter of Ituri province, the number of new cases being recorded had not fallen on a national level. Advertisement "Assuming the outbreak is under control because some Ebola treatment centers are admitting fewer patients would be a mistake," MSF's emergency coordinator in DRC Anthony Kergosien said. "The outbreak is not shrinking, it is moving: South Ubangi has become the seventh affected province, while North Kivu now accounts for nearly half of all newly confirmed cases, with test positivity rising sharply in recent days," Kergosien said. He added that undetected chains of transmission had already taken hold in the worst-hit areas, and said "the spread of the outbreak into new areas with even weaker preparedness and response capacities poses a serious risk." Incidental factors like the school year restarting this month provide new potential transmission risksImage: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance Which factors helped DRC's worst Ebola outbreak spread so fast? The deadly virus has killed more than 3,500 people from more than 7,200 confirmed cases since the outbreak was declared in May, according to WHO figures. Based on the recorded data, the quality of which is gradually improving with the passage of time, the 2026 outbreak is the fastest-spreading in history. It's also the largest in the DRC's history, second in overall size only to the West African outbreak of 2013-2016. The West African outbreak needed around two and a half years to reach a caseload of more than 28,000, not four months to pass 7,000. Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 12:34 Many of the cases have been concentrated in hard-to-reach areas in DRC's north and east long plagued by instability, poor health infrastructure and a series of armed groups. Medical staff strikes have also contributed to problems fighting the spread, as have dearly-held funeral and burial traditions that pose the risk of post-mortem transmission as people bid their loved ones farewell. The outbreak also involves a rare Ebolavirus strain, Bundibugyo, meaning that existing treatments and vaccines — several of which are prohibitively expensive by the standards of the region anyway — were untested and of uncertain value against it. All rights reserved By Giedre Peseckyte Published on 21/09/2026 - 17:16 GMT+2 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Two European epidemiologists are going to the epicentre of the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In the meantime, clinical trials of the Ervebo vaccine kick off. Two European epidemiologists are heading to the epicentre of the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) is sending two experts “to reinforce surveillance and overall outbreak response,” the EU agency’s chief, Pamela Rendi-Wagner, said in a press release on Monday. The Centre has been providing direct support since the current outbreak began, with experts deployed since May to support the Africa CDC. In June, the Centre led an assessment of exit screening at airports in the DRC and Uganda, while experts have also been deployed to South Sudan. The latest health authority data indicates more than 7,600 confirmed cases of infection, including over 3,670 deaths, with nearly eight in 10 infections recorded in Ituri. The outbreak “has already cost so many lives,” Rendi-Wagner said. The ECDC says the risk to Europeans remains very low. The virus spreads between humans through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people. It can also be transmitted by contact with bedding or clothing contaminated with these fluids. While “sporadic importations” to the European Union could occur, “multiple independent importations are unlikely even in a pessimistic scenario in which the number of cases continue to rise in the affected regions,” the agency said. Related Congo begins Ebola vaccinations against world's fastest-growing outbreak Clinical trials to kick off On the same day, the World Health Organisation announced that a research vaccination programme for the Ervebo vaccine — the only licensed Ebola vaccine — has begun in Ituri for health workers and other frontline personnel at increased risk of exposure. 20,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine have been allocated to study whether the vaccine protects against the Bundibugyo virus, which is causing the current outbreak and has no licensed vaccine or treatment. That's part of the total of 70,000 doses that have been made available to the Congolese authorities to support the outbreak response and related research. The vaccine was “highly effective” against Ebola Zaire virus in the past, but it is not yet known whether it can provide “meaningful protection” against Ebola Bundibugyo disease, which is still spreading in the DRC, the United Nations said in a press release. records.content: 2 0 comment Listen ~4 min TrialSite Staff | Making Biomedical Research Evidence Accessible to All Sep. 21, 2026, 4:00 p.m. The Democratic Republic of Congo has expanded Ebola vaccination as its massive 2026 Bundibugyo virus outbreak continues, with more than 3,700 people receiving Ervebo, Merck’s licensed Ebola vaccine. But this is also a major real-world scientific test: Ervebo is licensed against Zaire ebolavirus, not Bundibugyo virus, and whether it protects humans against the latter remains unknown. The newly launched BRAVO study, led by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) and its epidemiological research arm Epicentre within the Congolese Ministry of Health response, plans to follow 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu for nine to 12 months to determine whether vaccination reduces disease or severe outcomes. The effort has a significant biodefense and health-security dimension. Ebola vaccines are not conventional mass-market products: governments, international organizations and preparedness programs maintain countermeasures so they can be deployed rapidly when outbreaks occur. The Gavi-funded global Ebola vaccine stockpile maintains a target of 500,000 Ervebo doses, with some inventory pre-positioned in DRC. Its origins trace to Gavi’s advance-purchase commitment during the 2014–2016 West African Ebola crisis, which helped create a guaranteed market while Ervebo was still investigational. For the current emergency, the International Coordinating Group on Vaccine Provision—comprising WHO, UNICEF, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and MSF, with Gavi financing the stockpile—released 70,000 Ervebo doses. Approximately 50,000 are allocated for healthcare and frontline workers and 20,000 for a Phase 3 clinical trial. Gavi committed about $7 million for the doses and another $6 million for outbreak preparedness and immunization support. The preparedness effort extends beyond Ervebo. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) has committed another $4.17 million to research teams at UCLA, the Institute of Tropical Medicine Antwerp, University of Oxford and MRC-University of Glasgow Centre for Virus Research to investigate whether existing Ebola vaccines generate immunity against Bundibugyo virus. CEPI is separately supporting development of Bundibugyo-specific vaccines, while Gavi has committed $40 million through its First Response Fund toward accelerating access to candidate vaccines. BRAVO launched September 19 at the WHO-run health-worker training center in Bunia. Initial vaccination in Ituri is being deployed through a fixed site at the Ituri Provincial Laboratory and the Elikya Ebola Treatment Center in Bunia, with plans to expand to additional Ebola treatment centers and eventually Mongbwalu. Bunia and Mongbwalu are among the outbreak's major affected zones. These sites sit within a much larger clinical-research network. The separate PARTNERS treatment trial was operating at five clinical-management facilities in Ituri and had enrolled more than 300 confirmed patients by early September. Dr. Placide Mbala of DRC's National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB) has been identified publicly as a leader of the country's therapeutic clinical-trial effort. The immediate commercial market is unusual: Ebola vaccination is largely a government-, donor- and preparedness-driven countermeasure market, not a traditional consumer vaccine market. The 500,000-dose global stockpile provides a clearer measure of baseline preparedness demand than conventional patient-market calculations. But if Ervebo demonstrates meaningful cross-protection against Bundibugyo virus, its strategic value could expand substantially—potentially turning an Ebola Zaire-specific asset into a broader filovirus preparedness tool. That possibility remains unproven. WHO is explicit on that point: animal and immunological evidence suggests possible cross-protection, but current evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful protection in humans. Ervebo should therefore be used against Bundibugyo only within research protocols while rigorous effectiveness and randomized-trial evidence is generated. © 2026 TrialSite News®. All rights reserved. records.content: Skip to main content Global editionWednesday, September 23, 2026 Streamline Search⌘KWriteSign inJoin Streamline StreamlineGlobal edition LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSportDirectoryHouse HuntingPeopleHistoryMore LatestWorldBusinessPoliticsTechnologyScienceCultureSport Back to News/Health Health Congo begins Ebola vaccinations for frontline workers in Ituri Congo started vaccinating frontline workers in Bunia with the Ervebo shot as the deadliest Ebola outbreak in its history reaches 3,639 deaths. Streamline Feed OfficialVerified Sep 20, 2026Updated Sep 20, 20264 min read Report article Follow on Google News Try askingWhy does this matter? Advertisement from Kings Summit. The first 10 seconds cannot be skipped. Ad playing Ad playing. Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Congo began vaccinating health and other frontline workers against Ebola on Saturday in Bunia, the epicentre of the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in the country's history, as government figures put the death toll at 3,639. Health authorities are prioritising frontline workers for the Ervebo vaccine, which proved effective in previous outbreaks caused by the more common Zaire strain of the virus. The initial rollout targets the Bunia and Mongbwalu health zones in Ituri province, both among the areas hardest hit by the current epidemic, authorities said on Saturday. Nikole Landu, a healthcare worker who received a dose, said she sought vaccination because she is in constant contact with sick people and at high risk of catching the disease. "So the vaccine I received today will help protect me. I might still get the disease, but I'm less likely to develop a severe case," she said. A vaccine built for a different virus The campaign's central scientific question is whether Ervebo works against the virus now circulating. The vaccine proved effective against Zaire ebolavirus, the strain behind most past outbreaks. Health authorities said it could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus driving the current epidemic because the two viruses are related, but whether it actually prevents illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied. Because of that uncertainty, the vaccine is being deployed under a compassionate-use program, an arrangement that allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use. The approach trades certainty for speed: instead of waiting for strain-specific evidence, authorities are deploying the vaccine while studies assess whether it works. The campaign will therefore double as a real-world evaluation of cross-protection, with results shaping whether the effort is expanded or reconsidered. The outbreak at a glance As of Saturday, the country had recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, according to government figures. The outbreak is concentrated in Ituri province, and it is already the deadliest of the 17 Ebola outbreaks recorded in the country. Dividing the reported deaths by confirmed cases yields a case-fatality ratio of roughly 48 percent, a Streamline calculation based on the government figures; the true ratio may differ because the count excludes probable and suspected cases. Key figures for the Ebola outbreak, Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo Measure Value Status and source Confirmed cases 7,541 Government figures as of Saturday, reported September 20, 2026 Confirmed deaths 3,639 Government figures as of Saturday, reported September 20, 2026 Case-fatality ratio among confirmed cases About 48 percent Streamline calculation from government figures; excludes probable and suspected cases Outbreak rank Deadliest of 17 in the country Health authorities 2014-2016 West Africa comparison More than 11,000 deaths Deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, mainly Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone The World Health Organization has said the outbreak remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. That projection is a warning rather than an outcome: the Ituri toll is still well below the West African one, and the trajectory will depend on how quickly vaccination, case-finding and treatment can gain ground. Delivery under pressure The rollout begins amid what health authorities describe as extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. Each factor works against containment: displacement and constant movement raise the risk that infections surface far from treatment, insecurity makes it harder for response teams to reach affected communities, and the strike involves the same healthcare workforce the campaign depends on to run vaccination sites and trace contacts. The choice of who gets vaccinated first reflects that arithmetic. Frontline workers face the highest exposure because they treat patients, which is why authorities put them ahead of the wider population. Their protection also matters for the response itself: an unprotected workforce cannot safely staff treatment centres, and further deaths among health workers would deepen a staffing strain already worsened by industrial action. What to watch The immediate test is delivery: whether doses reach frontline workers across the Bunia and Mongbwalu zones quickly enough to blunt transmission in the epidemic's fastest-moving areas. The decisive unknown is scientific. Whether Ervebo prevents illness in people infected with the Bundibugyo virus remains under study, and the answer will determine how much confidence the effort can claim. For now, the country's deadliest Ebola epidemic has a vaccination campaign in its epicentre, one whose effectiveness is hoped for rather than proven. How did this story land? No sign-in required. OffOn Stream on Scientists warn of weakening health systems and urge stronger outbreak detection West African laboratory scientists are urging governments to strengthen their capacity to detect disease outbreaks to prevent another major crisis ByERICK KAGLAN Associated Press September 18, 2026, 10:38 PM LOME, Togo -- LOME, Togo (AP) — West African laboratory scientists called on governments Friday to strengthen capacity to detect disease outbreaks to avoid another major outbreak, saying health systems across the region are becoming weaker. The scientists issued their warning in Togo's capital, Lome, where they have gathered this week to discuss the region's level of preparation for disease outbreaks and dependence on vaccines from Western countries. They said governments in the region have to cooperate to strengthen disease detection and invest in diagnostic capacities, citing lessons from Ebola and COVID-19 outbreaks that the region has grappled with in the past decade. Between 2014 and 2016, an Ebola outbreak killed at least 11,000 people across West Africa, overwhelmingly in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. “We need to anticipate these outbreaks,” said Kossi Kabo, the head of the Association of Medical Biologists of Togo and a co-chair of the congress. “We shouldn’t wait for an epidemic to emerge somewhere before responding. By then, it would be too late.” Popular Reads Strait of Hormuz shut until Tehran's conditions met, Ghalibaf says Sep 20 Cindy Crawford's son Presley Gerber dies at 27 2 days ago Twin sisters conjoined at head underwent successful separation surgery: Hospital Sep 16 Africa as a whole remains at risk for outbreaks. The rare Bundibugyo virus has killed over 3,600 people among nearly 7,500 cases in Congo since mid-May, when Congolese authorities announced a fresh deadly Ebola outbreak. The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the tolls are likely three times the official figures and the outbreak is already history's fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak. The virus spread without detection for several weeks. Also, Hantavirus was detected on a cruise ship that docked in the Atlantic off Cape Verde in May. Scientists are worried that in the absence of a major outbreak threatening the region, maintenance of the health systems has waned, leaving them unprepared for potential future epidemics. Arthur Bodurie Calvin Garber, president of the Sierra Leone Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists, said the governments must also invest in people as much as infrastructure. Britannica Editors Last updated Sep. 19, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Viewed through an electron microscope, ebolaviruses appear as long filaments, sometimes branched or intertwined. The virion (virus particle) contains one molecule of noninfectious single-stranded RNA (ribonucleic acid). It is not known how the viruses attack cells; it has been postulated that they produce proteins that suppress the immune system, allowing reproduction of virus to continue unhindered. Viral hemorrhagic fevers similar to Ebola typically are carried by arthropods and rodents, but the natural reservoirs for ebolaviruses are yet to be discovered. Among the suspected reservoirs for Ebola are bats, primates, rodents, and insects that inhabit tropical forests in Africa and Asia. Ebola can be transmitted through contact with infected blood and bodily fluids as well as through contact with surfaces or objects contaminated by those fluids. The virus has also been detected in the organs of patients after recovery from the fever. In men, the virus may remain infectious in semen for as long as two months following return to health. Unsanitary conditions and lack of adequate medical supplies may be factors in the spread of the disease. Burial rituals that involve close contact with the body of a person who has died from the disease also can result in the spread of Ebola. The surfaces of bodies of deceased victims remain infectious for more than a week. In addition, a small percentage of Ebola-infected individuals may remain asymptomatic; such persons may unknowingly carry and spread the virus. Ebolaviruses have an incubation period of 2 to 21 days. The onset of illness is sudden and harsh. Infected persons may develop fever, severe headaches and muscle aches, and loss of appetite. Within a few days the virus causes a condition known as disseminated intravascular coagulation, which is marked by both blood clots and hemorrhaging. In the case of Ebola, clots are concentrated in the liver, spleen, brain, and other internal organs, forcing capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea with blood and mucus, conjunctivitis, and sore throat soon follow. A maculopapular rash (discolored elevations of the skin) appears on the trunk and quickly spreads to the limbs and head. The patient is then beset by spontaneous bleeding from body orifices and any breaks in the skin, such as injection sites, and within the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Death is usually brought on by hemorrhaging, shock, or renal failure and occurs within 8 to 17 days. Persons who survive Ebola infection may experience post-Ebola syndrome, symptoms of which include vision problems (potentially blindness), headaches, severe joint and muscle pain, and extreme fatigue. Treatment Treatment for Ebola is primarily with supportive care, including fluids, electrolytes, and medications to stabilize blood pressure and manage complications. Early treatment greatly improves survival. For infections caused by the Zaire strain of Ebola virus, targeted antibody therapies such as REGN-EB3 (Inmazeb) and mAb114 (Ebanga) can help reduce mortality. Other treatments that had been investigated for Ebola included the antiviral drug remdesivir (RDV) and ZMapp, a mixture of three antibodies that bind to proteins on ebolaviruses. ZMapp was administered to infected individuals during the 2014–16 outbreak, though its effectiveness was unclear. In trials during the 2018–20 Ebola outbreak, both REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were found to be more effective at reducing Ebola-related mortality compared with RDV and ZMapp. REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2020. Ebola virus disease; hand washingA Liberian nurse washing his hands with water after treating a patient sick with Ebola virus disease in Monrovia, Liberia, during the 2014–15 outbreak.(more) The spread of ebolaviruses can be contained by barrier nursing, handling of infected blood and tissue in isolated laboratory units, and proper decontamination of reusable equipment. Experimental vaccines are under development for Ebola, including a vaccine known as VSV-EBOV, which was found to be highly effective in preventing the spread of ebolavirus among persons in close contact with infected individuals. VSV-EBOV was a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV)-based vaccine that expressed an EBOV glycoprotein. When VSV-EBOV was injected, the vaccinated individuals generated antibodies against the EBOV protein, thereby gaining immunity. Survivors of Ebola infection may be affected by a constellation of long-term health complications known as post-Ebola syndrome. In follow-up studies of persons who recovered from acute Ebola infection, many were found to suffer from uveitis (eye redness and pain), vision loss, tinnitus, hearing loss, stroke, headaches, muscle and joint pain, and other abnormalities in musculoskeletal and neurological function. Some affected individuals also suffered renal failure and were at increased risk of premature death. Post-Ebola syndrome is treated primarily by symptom management with drugs such as analgesics (pain relievers) and anti-inflammatory agents. Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Top Questions What are viral hemorrhagic fevers? Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of highly dangerous illnesses caused by viruses that damage the vascular system, leading to severe bleeding. Initial symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, and exhaustion. These viruses belong to four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. Specific animals or insects often transmit them, restricting these diseases to certain geographic areas. Examples include dengue, yellow fever, Lassa fever, and Ebola. Transmission to humans usually occurs via contact with infected animals like rodents and insects. Avoiding contact with these hosts and controlling their populations can prevent infection. Isolation of infected individuals can also prevent the virus from spreading from person to person. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. Which viruses can cause viral hemorrhagic fevers? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of severe illnesses characterized by bleeding, fever, and shock. These diseases are caused by viruses from four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. Flaviviruses Dengue and yellow fever viruses, often transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, are the most common causes. While yellow fever affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue induces only minor bleeding but can result in dengue shock syndrome. Arenaviruses are spread to humans through contact with food or soil contaminated by rodent excreta. This family of viruses causes Lassa fever, Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever. Bunyaviridae includes Hantaviruses, Rift Valley fever virus, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. Hantaviruses are transmitted to humans through rodent contact, while Rift Valley fever is a mosquito-borne disease. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is a tick-borne disease. Filoviruses such as Ebola virus and Marburg virus, are highly fatal and may also cause disease in primates. The origin of filovirus epidemics remains unclear, but scientists suspect that fruit bats may be responsible for outbreaks of Marburg disease. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How do viral hemorrhagic fevers affect the human body? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of highly dangerous illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that harm the vascular system, resulting in significant bleeding. Initial symptoms include fever, fatigue, and muscle aches. The viruses attack cells and may suppress the immune system, which allows the virus to reproduce. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, a condition marked by blood clots and hemorrhaging, can occur. Clots concentrated in organs force capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. This leads to bleeding from body openings, the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Some VHFs, such as dengue, induce only minor bleeding that is rarely fatal, while others, such as Ebola, can cause death in up to 90% of victims. 4 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever Ebola: Course of infection Marburgvirus bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What role do blood vessels play in the disease process? In viral hemorrhagic fevers, blood vessels play a central role in the disease process. These diseases are caused by bloodborne viruses that damage the vascular system, leading to extensive bleeding internally, externally, and under the skin. Symptoms often include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, and exhaustion. These viruses are typically transmitted to humans via animals such as rodents and insects. There are no vaccines available, and treatment is mainly supportive. Preventing infection involves avoiding contact with host species and controlling rodent and insect populations. Isolation of infected individuals can also prevent human-to-human spread through physical contact. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. Why do people with these fevers sometimes bleed or bruise easily? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that damage the vascular system. This damage leads to bleeding under the skin, in internal organs, and from body orifices. Several factors contribute to the ease of bleeding and bruising: * Vascular Damage VHFs can cause vascular damage. * Coagulation Abnormalities Viral infections can cause abnormalities in blood clotting. * Cytokine Release Unregulated cytokine production may lead to vascular damage and hemorrhaging. Some VHFs are highly fatal; certain Ebola strains have mortality rates of up to 90%. Isolation of infected individuals helps prevent the spread of VHFs, as transmission can occur through physical contact. 3 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever Marburgvirus bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How does the body respond to fight off a viral hemorrhagic fever? Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of severe illnesses caused by various virus families that damage the vascular system, leading to bleeding. The body's response involves several complex mechanisms. The infection typically begins with the virus entering the body through contact with an infected animal or insect. Once inside, the virus targets cells in the vascular system, such as endothelial cells, which line blood vessels. The damage to these cells leads to increased vascular permeability and impaired blood clotting. This results in both internal and external hemorrhaging, as blood leaks from the vessels. The immune system responds by releasing cytokines, which are signaling molecules that help coordinate the immune response. However, in severe cases, this can lead to a "cytokine storm," where an excessive amount of cytokines are released, causing inflammation, shock, and organ failure. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases This answer is created from Britannica articles using AI. Show more Show less viral hemorrhagic fever, any of a variety of highly fatal viral diseases that are characterized by massive external or internal bleeding or bleeding into the skin. Other symptoms vary by the type of viral hemorrhagic fever but often include fever, malaise, muscle aches, vomiting, and shock. Most viral hemorrhagic fevers are geographically restricted because they are transmitted by specific animal or insect hosts (reservoirs) that occupy narrow and sometimes localized ecological niches. Viral hemorrhagic fevers are caused by viruses of four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. The most common viral hemorrhagic fevers are dengue and yellow fever, caused by related mosquito-borne flaviviruses, often being transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. In the late 18th century, yellow fever epidemics in American coastal cities caused widespread panic, but the disease currently occurs only in developing countries of Africa and South America. It is the only major viral hemorrhagic fever for which an effective preventive vaccine exists and is widely used. Most cases of dengue, seen in tropical areas, are mild and influenza-like, but all four dengue viruses may produce dengue hemorrhagic fever or its severe form, dengue shock syndrome. Unlike yellow fever, which affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue involves the liver only minimally and tends to induce only minor bleeding that is rarely fatal. However, if dengue shock syndrome occurs, patients may die when fluids and electrolytes in their vascular compartments shift into tissues, collapsing the blood volume and precipitating low blood pressure and shock. Dengue is unique among the fatal hemorrhagic fevers in that even severe cases can be effectively treated with simple fluid administration. The arenaviruses are highly adapted to specific rodent hosts, which may become silently infected and excrete the virus in feces, urine, and saliva. However, when humans come into contact with food or soil contaminated by these rodent excreta, disease may result. The arenaviruses cause the diseases Lassa fever (occurring in Africa), Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever. Health authorities said Saturday that the campaign targets Bunia and Mongbwalu, two of the areas hardest hit by the virus, and is expected to cover 20,000 frontline workers in Ituri and North Kivu provinces over a period of six to nine months. The military governor of Ituri Province, Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, said the workers are being prioritized because of their heightened exposure to the risk of infection and their direct involvement in responding to the outbreak. The Ervebo vaccine is licensed to prevent disease caused by the Zaire ebolavirus and has been proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola. However, its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus causing the current outbreak remains under study, Mulumba added. He noted that there is currently no licensed vaccine or specific treatment for the virus causing the current outbreak. The official in charge of the health response in the DRC, Prof. Steve Ahuka, said the vaccine's effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus remains unknown. According to the latest figures released by the Congolese National Institute of Public Health, the country has recorded 7,541 confirmed cases, including 3,639 deaths, accounting for about 48.3% of the recorded cases. A total of 1,823 patients have recovered, with the outbreak spreading to seven provinces. The outbreak began in Ituri Province and was officially declared in mid-May, becoming the deadliest Ebola outbreak the country has experienced. The World Health Organization (WHO) announced in August that it had allocated 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine to the DRC, including 50,000 doses for health workers and frontline workers and 20,000 doses for a clinical trial to study the level of protection the vaccine provides against the Bundibugyo virus. The vaccine had already begun to be used last month in the city of Kisangani in Tshopo Province, as part of a campaign scheduled to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces. According to the Congolese National Institute of Public Health, more than 3,000 people in Tshopo Province and more than 700 people in Bas-Uele Province have already received the vaccine. The UN World Health Organization announced on Monday that 20,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine have been allocated for the research vaccination program in Ituri province, the worst-hit region. The aim of the trial is to improve understanding of how effective the vaccine is against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, and to protect individuals most exposed to it. The Ervebo vaccine has been highly effective against Ebola Zaire virus in the past, but it is not yet known whether it can provide meaningful protection against Ebola Bundibugyo disease, which is still spreading in the DR Congo. A total of 70,000 doses have been made available to the Congolese authorities to support the outbreak response and related research, WHO said. The epicentre of the outbreak remains Ituri province in eastern DR Congo, although the virus has spread to seven provinces since it was confirmed in May this year. Those leading the outbreak response face many challenges related to an ongoing humanitarian emergency caused by decades of violence in the country's vast, resource-rich eastern provinces. Latest health authority data indicates a total of more than 7,600 confirmed cases of infection including over 3,670 deaths, with nearly eight in 10 infections recorded in Ituri. Ervebo is the only Ebola vaccine licensed for use during outbreaks caused by Bundibugyo virus. The WHO-backed panel, which advises on vaccines recommended earlier this month that Ervebo should only be used for research purposes initially. It also emphasized that the vaccine's "unknown efficacy" against Bundibugyo virus should be clearly communicated, although limited data and anecdotal reports suggest that Ervebo may provide "some protection" against the disease. Het Instituut voor Tropische Geneeskunde (ITG) in Antwerpen (België) zet zich sinds 1906 in voor de vooruitgang van wetenschap en gezondheid voor iedereen, via innovatief onderzoek, geavanceerd onderwijs, professionele medische dienstverlening en capaciteitsuitwisseling met partnerinstellingen in Afrika, Azië en Latijns-Amerika. Ons doel is de wereldwijde impact van ziekten en gezondheidsproblemen op bevolkingsgroepen te verminderen. Wetenschappelijke excellentie en maatschappelijke relevantie zijn voor ons twee kanten van dezelfde medaille. Over het ITG Het ITG viert 120 jaar wetenschap Al meer dan een eeuw zet het Instituut voor Tropische Geneeskunde (ITG) zich in voor betere gezondheid en wetenschap in de wereld, via baanbrekend onderzoek, toonaangevend onderwijs en wereldwijde zorgverlening. Tijdens ons jubileumjaar blikken we terug op waar het begon en richten we ons op een toekomst die gevormd zal worden door onze grensverleggende doorbraken. Vier met ons mee In de kijker Gezocht: kunstenaar uit DRC die kritisch reflecteert op het ITG's koloniaal erfgoed We zoeken een kunstenaar (residentie) uit de DRC om kritisch te reflecteren op de kunstwerken van Fernand Allard l'Olivier en de bredere vragen die ze oproepen over institutioneel geheugen, koloniaal erfgoed en de blijvende impact van kolonialisme op het heden. Het ITG-boek – nu verkrijgbaar! Het langverwachte boek over het ITG is er! records.content: Menu Close Up-to-Date Information, Close to the Community. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Discover more vaccine Consult Online Doctors Ekonomi Home Health WHO Warns Ebola Epidemic Ongoing Despite Progress in Congo WHO Warns Ebola Epidemic Ongoing Despite Progress in Congo Ashley Morgan Published Sep 17, 2026 - 15:03 2 Reads Last Update Sep 17, 2026 - 15:03 Share WhatsApp Smallest Font Largest Font Medical containment measures against the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo show signs of gaining ground, though global health officials warned on Wednesday that the ongoing outbreak remains far from over. Data reported by Congo as of September 11 indicates more than 7,000 confirmed Ebola cases. The outbreak, which stands as the second most lethal on record, has now reached its seventh province. Declines in virus transmission have been observed in heavily affected areas of Ituri province. However, high population mobility across the region poses a continued risk of further spreading the virus. "We are now starting to see encouraging signs that we are gaining ground," said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General, World Health Organization. Surveillance and contact-tracing operations are expanding across affected zones, which health authorities note could lead to an initial rise in newly identified cases. "We have many, many months ahead of us," said Maria Van Kerkhove, acting director of epidemic and pandemic threat management, World Health Organization. "This is far from over." Response efforts include the administration of Merck's Ervebo vaccine to over 3,000 healthcare and frontline workers. While Ervebo is licensed for Zaire ebolavirus, its efficacy against the current outbreak's driving strain, the Bundibugyo virus, remains unproven. Health officials plan to launch an observational study involving frontline workers to evaluate vaccine effectiveness. Additionally, a mid-to-late-stage clinical trial led by Congo's National Institute of Biomedical Research and international partners will begin in the coming weeks. "Ervebo will be among the first vaccines evaluated for efficacy in the trial, followed by other vaccine candidates specifically targeting Bundibugyo Ebola," said Meg Doherty, director of science, research, evidence and quality for health, World Health Organization. Subsequent testing phases within the trial will assess additional vaccine candidates, including developments from Moderna and the University of Oxford. Learn more IOM Results Portal Visit website IOM Annual Report 2025 Visit website Download Annual Report 2025 Ebola Outbreak 2026: How IOM is Helping The Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) continues to escalate, reaching 7,672 confirmed cases, 3,699 deaths, and 1,879 recoveries, with an overall Case Fatality Rate (CFR) of 48.2%. Live update Donate now 75 years of trust 75 Years of Trust. A Future of Impact. The story of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) is one of people moving forward – through crises, change and new beginnings – shaping safer, more humane mobility worldwide. IOM’s 75th Anniversary is a unique moment to highlight IOM’s policy impact, operational results, financial discipline, and future readiness. See timeline Why IOM matters When IOM Helps People Return, With Dignity Whatever path brought someone to the point of needing our help – a shipwreck, a stalled journey, years of hardship abroad – our teams meet them there, with kindness, with healthcare, counselling, and honest information to help them decide what comes next for themselves. By Carlos Oliver Cruz Chief of Mission, IOM Egypt Read article Staying Through the Storm: How IOM Supports Migrants in Yemen We don't just show up in the worst moment and disappear. We stay through the in-between, when someone is no longer in crisis, but not yet strong enough to stand on their own two feet. By Abdusattor Esoev Chief of Mission, IOM Yemen Read article Finding My Place in Humanitarian Security I joined IOM in 2021, working first on the Community Feedback Mechanism. What struck me immediately was the working environment. There were women throughout the office, including in senior leadership, and I felt respected and encouraged to speak up. By Wed Saleh Junior Security Assistant, IOM Yemen Read article Be a lifeline to people in need Lifeline With your help, IOM can save lives by delivering crucial assistance wherever and whenever it is needed most. Read More Edit See moreExplainer Every story Matters. Wherever you’re from, the game finds you. The world’s game has always travelled. So have we. Wherever you’re from, the game finds you. every team is made of journeys. football needs the whole world to play so it does. Take the quiz Question 1 / 5 How many national teams belong to FIFA, football's world body? Next Question 100 150 211 211, which is even more than the number of countries in the United Nations. Almost every corner of the world plays this game. Finish Question 2 / 5 How many countries are hosting the 2026 World Cup together? Next Question One Two Three Three: Canada, Mexico and the United States. For the first time ever, three nations share the tournament between them. Finish Question 3 / 5 How many teams are playing in the 2026 World Cup, the biggest one yet? Finish 24 32 48 48 teams, more than ever before. More teams means more journeys, and more of the world on one stage. Finish Question 4 / 5 Which of these stars grew up in a family with a story of migration? Finish Kylian Mbappé Lamine Yamal Jamal Musiala All of them All of them. Mbappé's father came from Cameroon, and Kylian now leads France. Lamine Yamal's parents came from Morocco and Equatorial Guinea, and he stars for Spain, where he was born. Musiala's father is from Nigeria, and Jamal now plays for Germany. Different journeys, one game we all love. Finish Question 5 / 5 In football, what is always on the move? Finish The ball The players The fans All of them All of them. Players, fans, and the ball itself are always travelling. The game is built on journeys. Finish Congratulations! You completed the quiz. Football brings the world together. Players come from every corner of the earth, fans cheer from every continent, and the game grows richer for it. We believe that every person's story matters, and that communities are at their strongest when everyone feels they belong. Migration connects people, cultures, and opportunities. On the pitch and off it, we are all part of the same team. Our offices worldwide IOM currently has operations in 171 countries through more than 520 field offices across six regions.
